lead: A conditional random field (CRF) is a sequence model that scores a whole label sequence y for a sentence x with one log-linear function and normalises once over every possible sequence. It exists because per-position classifiers in a maximum entropy Markov model normalise each step alone, so a confident early step can hide later evidence. A linear-chain CRF fixes that by making complete sequences compete. Taggers use it for part-of-speech, chunking, named entities and any task where neighbouring labels depend on each other.
prereq: You need 2.6 for log-linear scoring and label bias, and 2.5 for Viterbi decoding.

sections.h3: One score for the whole label sequence

blocks.text: A conditional random field (CRF) models P(y | x) directly. Here x = (x₁, ..., xₙ) is the observed sentence and y = (y₁, ..., yₙ) is a label sequence such as tags. A linear-chain CRF is an undirected graphical model: the labels form a chain, and each label may look at the whole observation x. The chain keeps inference tractable while still allowing overlapping features.
P(y | x) = (1 / Z(x)) exp( Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> Σ<sub>j=1</sub><sup>m</sup> λ<sub>j</sub> f<sub>j</sub>(y<sub>i−1</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>, x, i) )
blocks.where: y is the label sequence; x is the sentence; n is the number of tokens; m is the number of feature functions; f<sub>j</sub> is feature function j; λ<sub>j</sub> is its weight; y<sub>0</sub> = START; Z(x) is the partition function.

blocks.text: The exponent is the sequence score S(y, x) = Σ<sub>i</sub> Σ<sub>j</sub> λ<sub>j</sub> f<sub>j</sub>(y<sub>i−1</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>, x, i). A feature function returns a number, often 0 or 1, from the previous label, the current label, the whole sentence and the position. The weight says how useful that feature is.
Z(x) = Σ<sub>y′ ∈ Y(x)</sub> exp( S(y′, x) )
blocks.where: Y(x) is the set of all possible label sequences for x; with two labels and n tokens, |Y(x)| = 2ⁿ.

blocks.text: No position is normalised alone. A high score at token 1 is weighed against every complete sequence, including sequences with different later labels. This is the difference from the per-position normaliser in 2.6.

sections.h3: Decoding, the partition function and training

blocks.text: Z(x) sums over |Y|ⁿ label sequences, where |Y| is the number of labels — too many to list. The forward algorithm computes it in O(n |Y|²) by passing a vector of partial sums along the chain. Viterbi uses the same chain but replaces sum with max, returning argmax<sub>y</sub> P(y | x) in O(n |Y|²).

Training maximises conditional log-likelihood on tagged pairs (x, y): L = Σ log P(y | x) = Σ [S(y, x) − log Z(x)]. The gradient for λ<sub>j</sub> is the observed count of feature f<sub>j</sub> on the training sequence minus its expected count under the model, P(y′ | x). Forward-backward computes those expected counts. There is no closed form, so an iterative optimiser is used.

The price is slower training: every gradient step touches all labels through Z, and every new sentence needs its own Z. Training is heavier than an HMM or a per-position classifier. Decoding remains linear in sentence length for a fixed label set.

sections.h3: HMM, MEMM and CRF side by side

blocks.text: The three sequence models answer different questions. An HMM is generative: it models P(x, y) = P(y)P(x | y) and assumes observations are independent given the state. A maximum entropy Markov model (MEMM) is discriminative but normalises at each position, so a locally confident transition can hide evidence from later tokens. A CRF is discriminative and normalises once over whole sequences, which removes that label bias.
Read the table as a trade. Moving down adds feature freedom and global consistency, and adds computation.

figure.caption: Every complete label sequence adds its exponential into one sum, Z(x) = 30.00; out of that single pool the sequence N,V,N gets 12.18 ÷ 30.00 = 0.406. No position is normalised on its own.

examples.question: A linear-chain CRF has two labels, N and V. For a three-token sentence x, exp(S(N,V,N)) = 12.18, exp(S(N,N,N)) = 6.05, and the other six label sequences have exponentials summing to 11.77. Find Z(x) and P(N,V,N | x).
steps: There are 2³ = 8 label sequences because each of the 3 tokens takes 2 labels.
Z(x) is the sum over all 8 sequences: Z = 12.18 + 6.05 + 11.77 = 30.00.
examples.check:
exp_nvn = 12.18
exp_nnn = 6.05
exp_other = 11.77
Z = exp_nvn + exp_nnn + exp_other
p = exp_nvn / Z
print(f'{Z:.2f}')
print(f'{p:.3f}')

traps: Z(x) is not the product of the per-position normalisers from 2.6. It is one sum over all complete label sequences, and it changes with x.
The score S(y, x) can be any real number; exp(S) is positive but not yet a probability. Divide by Z exactly once.
Set y₀ = START before the first token, or the first transition feature is missing. Do not drop the position i when a feature is position-specific.
Viterbi finds the highest-scoring label sequence. It does not compute Z, and the best path's score is not a probability until divided by Z.
Two labels and n tokens give 2ⁿ sequences, not 2n. For n = 3 the partition sum has 8 terms.

quiz.q: What is the partition function Z(x) in a linear-chain CRF?
quiz.a: Z(x) = Σ over all label sequences y′ of exp(S(y′, x)); it normalises the scores into probabilities.

quiz.q: Why does a CRF recompute Z for every input sentence?
quiz.a: Because the score and the set of possible sequences depend on x; Z(x) is a sum over y for that fixed x, not a constant table.

quiz.q: What does a feature function fⱼ return, and what does λⱼ do?
quiz.a: fⱼ returns a numeric feature value from yᵢ₋₁, yᵢ, x and i, often 0 or 1; λⱼ is its learned weight, so the product adds to the sequence score.

quiz.q: For one sentence, exp(S(N,V,N)) = 12.18 and Z(x) = 30.00. Find P(N,V,N | x).
A CRF has exp(S(y, x)) = 4.0 and Z(x) = 20.0. Find P(y | x) and the total probability of all other sequences.
quiz.a: P(y | x) = 4 / 20 = 0.20; the other sequences have total probability 1 − 0.20 = 0.80.

quiz.q: Why can a MEMM suffer label bias where a CRF does not?
quiz.a: A MEMM divides by a per-position normaliser, so a locally high-probability transition can be chosen without seeing later observations. A CRF divides once by Z(x), so every complete sequence competes with every other complete sequence.

quiz.q: Viterbi and the forward algorithm use the same weights. State one difference and one consequence.
quiz.a: Viterbi replaces sum with max and returns the best label sequence; forward sums and returns Z(x) for probabilities. Both take O(n |Y|²), where |Y| is the number of labels and n is the sentence length.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, linear-chain CRFs often sit on top of neural encoders such as BiLSTM or transformer layers; the CRF layer enforces valid label transitions and global consistency for entity spans. Bioinformatics uses CRFs for DNA and protein segmentation, and OCR uses them for character sequences. Search terms: linear-chain CRF forward-backward, BIO tagging CRF, and neural CRF. The same global-normalisation idea reappears in structured prediction beyond sequences, such as parse trees and image segmentation.
